text: 0 Casey For Oregon Take Action Casey For Oregon Take Action Issues Economy To bolster our Oregon economy, we must invest in a robust education system while fostering support from our local big and small businesses. Local businesses are the backbone of our future job market. We need to encourage and develop technological advances, expansion of labor resources, and improve infrastructure.

Enhancement in these areas promotes tremendous growth in our small and large businesses, leveraging our financial resources to uplift local enterprises, particularly in the sectors of manufacturing, agriculture, green technologies, and healthcare advances.. A thriving economy hinges on the vitality of small businesses, and I stand firmly in support of their success.

Education Education stands as the cornerstone of our communities' future. Today's industries demand highly skilled labor, and it's our responsibility to bridge that gap within our district. With some of the state's top educational institutions being one of the most diverse regions, we have the potential for incredible growth. By investing in our education system, we are laying the groundwork for our children's success and building a sustainable future in our community.

We need to invest in programs that align with our goals of supporting existing businesses, green technologies, and emerging industries. Also, I'm a steadfast supporter of teachers and committed to nurturing our youth. Prioritizing the safety of our students and educators is paramount.

Environment The environment requires our stewardship and attention. We need to research solutions that will combat climate change. We are short on time with some dramatic changes in our daily lives happening today; for example, wildfires are more frequent and more intense every year, and temperature swings are negatively impacting our forests and our agricultural community. We need to start addressing this as a threat to human life, so I support businesses using renewable technologies.

Oregon is known as the "Silicon Forest," and I support Oregonian’s efforts to lead the way in researching, studying, and promoting green technologies. Meeting our future needs with clean technologies and business practices will enhance all aspects of life. We need to keep moving forward on green initiatives.

Healthcare Ensuring accessibility to health care is paramount for every individual. It's not just a statewide issue but directly impacts every district member. As Oregonians, we have a duty to stand up for our neighbors and support our healthcare workers, especially after the challenges they faced during the COVID-19 pandemic.

Moving forward, it is imperative that we heed the advice of healthcare experts to shape policies that benefit both healthcare professionals and citizens alike, with an overall focus on increasing accessibility for every member of the district.

Affordable Housing and Community Safety Addressing housing demands remains a significant challenge both locally and nationally. My platform emphasizes maintaining positive momentum and implementing more extraordinary accountability measures to track the effectiveness of the allocated funds supporting families and individuals in difficult situations. Our focus should be facilitating pathways to housing and community stability and safety.
Promoting Equal Rights

I firmly reject discrimination across all aspects of life specifically including education, employment, healthcare, housing, and criminal justice. I'm dedicated to bolstering civil rights safeguards in combating discrimination and prejudice in our daily interactions. I will champion the rights of minorities and marginal communities, including women, people of color, LGBTQIA+ individuals, immigrants, and people with disabilities. I pledge to advocate for the safeguarding of these communities to guarantee equal access to resources, opportunities, and protections necessary for their well-being. Every individual deserves to be treated with dignity, respect, and equality.

Supporting Unions I'm dedicated to promoting and safeguarding workers' rights. I value the indispensable role of our unions advocating for fair wages, safe working conditions, and well-being for all workers and their families. Workers should have a voice in the workplace, particularly concerning safety issues. The ability to collectively bargain and negotiate to improve wages, benefits, and working conditions helps all workers and our communities.
I acknowledge the pivotal role unions play in advancing economic justice and diminishing incoming inequality by empowering workers and amplifying their voices.

top of page The Issues A platform for humanity I have dedicated much of my adult life to the fight for human rights and dignity. Together, as your representative, we can work to pass transformative legislation which guarantees healthcare, housing, and ecological sustainability as human rights for everyone in our community.

I n a world of growing instability, inequality and intolerance, we must insist on the inherent worth and dignity of every human being regardless of their race, religion, gender, sexual orientation, level of ability, or any other social status. The policies listed below are my highest priorities that I believe I share with most Oregonians too. Please feel free to contact me if you would like to know more about my campaign, platform, or any issues not covered below.

Housing is a human right Housing is an essential need of every human being, yet many of us are severely burdened by the cost of housing. Worse still, families and neighbors who can't afford housing are criminalized simply for trying to survive. Whether you're sleeping in a tent, a vehicle, on a couch, or in your own house, housing is a human right, and I will fight to make sure that it is treated like one.
Establishing a right to rest , renter protections , and lifting the prohibition on local rent control will be my highest priorities.

Healthcare is a human right Oregon has made significant improvements to our healthcare system by making it both more accessible and more affordable. Still, so many in our community do not have the care they require. Whether people are uninsured or underinsured, our profit-driven healthcare system leaves hundreds of thousands of Oregon families to suffer needlessly. Even during this horrific pandemic, about eight percent of all Oregon families still don't have any health insurance.

This is devastating and could be completely resolved by switching to a single-payer – Medicare for All style – healthcare system , where everyone is completely covered and no one is left out. I will not compromise on access to reproductive healthcare, including abortion . I will not stop fighting until everyone has the care they need including vision , dental , and mental healthcare .

A Habitable Planet is a human right Climate change is no longer a problem of the future. We are living through worsening heat waves, historic wildfires, droughts, and many other extreme weather events that are only going to get worse unless we make a just green transition away from fossil fuels now. This means regulating big polluters while creating good jobs and ensuring that we have a safe landing place for workers currently employed in fossil fuel industries.

We need everything from regenerative agriculture to renewable energy production , climate smart transportation to waste management , and a focus on environmental justice for our society to be sustainable.

Unionization is a human right Everyone deserves dignity and respect on and off the job, and unions help with that. However, laws protecting the right to form a union leave out domestic, agricultural, construction and contract workers. Although unions are the best organizations to bring better wages and working conditions to all workers, we must address the exclusion of groups from this process and make it easier for workers to form unions free from intimidation and harassment.
We can improve our laws and reduce inequality here in Oregon by extending our state protections of workers' right to form a union to thousands of workers who don't have that now.

Education is a human right Education is the foundation of a well-functioning society and having a highly-skilled workforce provides immeasurable economic benefits. In Oregon, our education system has been hampered by a lack of funding from the state. We need to make Pre-K and Higher Education equally available to everyone , not just the well-off. We also need more funding to pay our teachers what they deserve and keep the promises that we've made to our students.

For too long big corporations have not been paying their fair share, while making billions in profits even during a pandemic. If we want a quality education system for Oregon, we need those who can most afford it – and those who have profited most from it – to pay it back to the community.

One of the major ways that big corporations have been able to avoid paying their fair share to fund Oregon schools, colleges and universities, is that they're able to hide how much profits they truly make in the state. We could fix that and see how much these mega-corporations are profiting in Oregon with a simple disclosure law, modeled after the 2018 Corporate Transparency and Accountability petition . bottom of page

Homes for all Everyone needs and deserves safe and affordable housing. In a district where one in three residents is rent-burdened, we must stop the skyrocketing costs of living and keep neighbors in our communities.

Housing Is a Human Right Housing is more than just shelter, it’s a fundamental necessity of life. Without it, meaningful participation in society is impossible. New York is facing a historic housing crisis because legislators in Albany, a quarter of whom are landlords , continue to put real estate profits over people. Nearly one in nine New York City students was homeless in 2023. One in three New York City tenants pay half their income in rent.
In Assembly District 37, 73% of households are renting, more than 45% of renters are rent-burdened or severely rent-burdened, and eviction filings more than doubled from 2021 to 2022.
In Ridgewood, where I live, rent is reaching historic highs, while rent stabilized apartments have been disappearing faster than anywhere in New York City.

Every person deserves a safe and affordable place to call home, regardless of their income or background. However in our current system, housing is prioritized as an instrument for profit and speculation, not as a universally necessary human right. This has led to skyrocketing rents, unjust evictions, and homelessness, especially among marginalized communities. Despite the fact that almost 70% of New Yorkers are renters, tenants’ rights are routinely disregarded, leaving many vulnerable to exploitation and displacement.

To address New York’s housing crisis, we need bold action that prioritizes people over real estate profits. Incremental changes won’t suffice; we must advocate for transformative policies – like real Good Cause eviction, Green Social Housing, fully funding NYCHA, expanded rent stabilization, the Housing Access Voucher Program, and the Tenant Opportunity to Purchase Act – that ensure everyone has access to permanently affordable housing and treat housing as a human right.

Building Tenant Power Good Cause Eviction Recently New York passed a watered down Good Cause Eviction bill that unfortunately leaves millions of New Yorkers unprotected. Good Cause has been a centerpiece of my campaign and passing the original, substantive bill is vital to ensuring Queens’ working families can stay in their homes.

Good Cause Eviction means exactly what it says: that landlords must have good cause to evict tenants, such as failing to pay rent or breaking a rule in their lease, and cannot simply evict for no reason at all. We need to pass the original legislation that protects tenants from unreasonable rent hikes and discriminatory evictions.

Expanding Rent Stabilization There are about a million rent stabilized apartments in New York City. This program is a lifeline to New Yorkers who would not be able to afford market-rate apartments. It is a program that we know works to keep communities whole and to provide long term security to working families. However, after decades, more and more apartments are falling out of stabilization, exacerbating New York’s housing crisis. We should expand stabilization to ensure New York is a city of working people, not just millionaires.

Tenant Opportunity to Purchase Act Tenants should never be displaced because landlords and speculators treat the housing market like a casino. The Tenant Opportunity to Purchase Act will give tenants the right to make the first offer if a building’s landlord decides to sell it. Not only would TOPA give tenants the opportunity to control their own futures, it would interrupt the union-busting associated with selling well-organized buildings.

Transitioning to a Just and Social Housing Economy Green Social Housing In a city where only around half of residential construction is built with union labor and over a third of renters spend 50% of their income on rent, it’s more important than ever to fight for healthy housing and good jobs. The Green Social Housing bill (A9088) would create the Social Housing Development Authority, a new agency that would build, acquire, rehabilitate, and finance high-quality, permanently affordable, sustainable housing.
Rent would be capped at 25% of a tenant’s income, and affordable financing would be available to tenants who wish to collectively purchase their buildings and turn them into co-ops.

Fund NYCHA NYCHA provides housing for one in 17 New Yorkers. Yet for the hundreds of thousands who live in NYCHA units, complaints abound of broken elevators, mold, and inhumane conditions after decades of disinvestment. Taxing the super-rich to fund NYCHA would bring necessary repairs and green retrofits to aging buildings, and guarantee safe, stable, and dignified housing for tenants.

Housing Access Voucher Program There are currently nearly 80,000 unhoused New Yorkers, with some studies showing the number as high as 146,000 . Seventy-eight percent of low-income tenants spend more than 30% of their income on rent. Over 100,000 children in NYC do not have a permanent place to call home. This is a crisis that we can and must solve.

The Housing Access Voucher Program will provide the most vulnerable New Yorkers – including low-income families facing eviction, unhoused people, or those facing a loss of housing due to domestic violence or hazardous living conditions – with the funds they desperately need to get into a stable, and safe home.

Green New York The climate crisis has arrived in our state and in Queens—and it’s getting worse. We need bold legislation that holds polluters accountable, upgrades our infrastructure, bans fossil fuels, and puts people and the planet first.

Power Is a Public Good Build Public Renewables Act In 2023, regular New Yorkers passed the largest Green New Deal victory in American history with the Build Public Renewables Act, which empowers the New York Power Authority to step in to build the publicly-owned clean energy we need to get New York off fossil fuels when the private sector falls short.

Now, we have to make sure New York uses BPRA to kick off the biggest buildout of renewable energy in history, all while lowering energy bills and creating tens of thousands of union jobs. BPRA will transform our climate, health, infrastructure, and economy, and I promise to fight to unlock its full potential and build renewables at the scale the climate crisis demands.

Lower Utility Bills We don’t have to depend on corporate monopolies for our energy. Con Ed and National Grid overcharge us, cut off power when we can’t pay outrageous premiums, keep us hooked on dirty fossil fuels, and neglect their infrastructure which results in blackouts. When rates go up, they profit, and working families suffer.
If we empower the New York Power Authority and transition to 100% democratically owned renewable energy, we will lower our bills and create a cleaner, healthier New York.

In addition, with BPRA, we established the REACH program to automatically discount energy bills of low- or moderate-income customers in disadvantaged communities, and I will be a voice for working families to ensure the program is done right. I will also support the New York HEAT Act, which caps utility bills at 6% for energy-burdened neighbors.

Green Union jobs The Green New York we deserve will be built by well-paid union workers. Transitioning to a just, renewable future with labor leading every step of the way is non-negotiable for me. We need to keep New Yorkers safe by building publicly owned renewable energy, building green social housing, and retrofitting existing buildings and schools to fortify our future.

These necessary projects will create tens of thousands of jobs in the process, and I will be fighting to ensure these are thriving-wage, union jobs that hire from communities who have been historically marginalized from the clean energy workforce.

Health Every New Yorker deserves to breathe clean air. But across the state and Queens, thousands of New Yorkers are struggling with asthma and dirty air because our state is still hooked on fossil fuels. It’s time to bring the smokestacks down. The Just Energy Transition Act (A4866) will jump-start the phase-out of our oldest and most-polluting fossil fuel plants, so that every New Yorker can breathe easy.

But right now New Yorkers in manufacturing zones across the state are forced to bear unchecked pollution from delivery trucks associated with the e-commerce mega-warehouses like Amazon that keep expanding in communities of color. The Clean Deliveries Act (A1718) would create protections for schools and disadvantaged neighborhoods, safeguarding our lungs from the air quality issues these warehouses have produced.

Green New Deal for Queens Green Social Housing The future is Green Social Housing built by the working class, for the working class, and owned by the working class. I will support the creation of a Social Housing Development Authority that will build and preserve permanently affordable housing that is publicly owned, tenant-controlled, union-built, and climate-resilient. See more here .

Clean, healthy homes should be for everyone — not just the rich. That’s why I also support the Green Affordable Pre-Electrification Program (A9170), which will provide funding for renovations to existing, older buildings that are often in need of weatherization and other energy efficiency improvements. This will make green homes accessible for working-class and low-income homeowners and renters, lower utility bills, and help New York achieve its climate goals.

With more than two thirds of New York City’s greenhouse emissions coming from buildings, combating climate change means we need to transition away from fossil fuel boilers and furnaces in our homes. The upgrades necessary to comply with Local Law 97 can be daunting, especially for New Yorkers on fixed incomes, working class families, and co-op shareholders living in older buildings.

That’s why I support the Bucks for Boilers Act (A9990), which would provide resources to households and building owners to make their homes more energy efficient and upgrade their gas boilers to electric heat pumps when it’s time to replace them.

The Bucks for Boilers Act would provide upfront costs to low-income New Yorkers who would otherwise not be able to make these necessary upgrades, and would require high-road labor standards for workers undertaking the upgrades—creating good, union jobs while ensuring that no one gets left behind in the transition to a renewable and green future.

Investing in public transit and bike lanes City planning shouldn’t prioritize cars over people. It’s time to shift gears towards pedestrian-friendly streets, ample green spaces, and efficient public transit . Let’s design cities that prioritize the well-being and accessibility of all residents, not just vehicles. By creating infrastructure that keeps everyone protected, we can create vibrant, livable communities where walking and cycling are safe and enjoyable. Investing in sustainable transportation options benefits our health, environment, and quality of life.

Climate resiliency We cannot slow-walk urgent infrastructure upgrades on behalf of the establishment’s fossil fuel donors. We must end our reliance on fossil fuels and protect people from the super storms they cause. That means retrofitting buildings and schools to make them safer and greener, and investing in green space, urban forests, and desperately needed flood mitigation.

More green space is not just good for the soul, it’s important for flood prevention. Queens needs flood mitigation as the climate crisis worsens. Green spaces can play a significant role in alleviating flooding, and urban forests have a big impact on flood control, allowing water to infiltrate into the soil instead of simply running off into streets or storm sewers.

I will also support state funding for an expanded tree initiative. In addition to reductions in four pollutants, (O3, NO2, SO2, PM10), carbon sequestration, decreased stormwater runoff, building energy savings due to shading, a 30% increase in tree coverage could lead to 40% fewer deaths from urban heat.
Workers Deserve It All We need to build a Queens for working families, not the 1%. That means fighting for higher wages, safer workplaces, and strong unions.

Fighting for Higher Wages and Better, Safer Workplaces Everything in our lives is made possible by the labor of workers, but bosses are hoarding wealth and squeezing us harder than ever — and they won’t give anything up without a fight. Workers shouldn’t have to scrape by, we need to thrive. I know what it’s like to live paycheck to paycheck, and I know the power of workers organizing together to get the compensation, protections, and respect they deserve.

Joining UAW Local 2110 changed my life, and I’m proud to be an elected leader and member of a union that’s fighting for the entire working class. As a legislator, I will fight for a strong labor movement, to raise the minimum wage, to end the sub-minimum wage, and to make billionaires pay their fair share — because you shouldn’t have to be rich to have a healthy, fulfilling life.

Raise the Minimum Wage While the costs of basic necessities reach historic highs, the super-rich suppress wages, raise rents and exploit workers. Raising the minimum wage to $25 is a fundamental step to building stability for working families.

EmPIRE Worker Protection Act Workers who witness unlawful or unsafe conditions in their workplace are often too scared of retaliation to take action—and in spite of New York State’s strong worker protections, our public agencies often lack the resources to enforce them.

The EmPIRE Act would enable workers to bring whistleblower lawsuits to address labor violations and wage theft in their workplace, even when they are not personally the target, and to collect a portion of the civil penalties imposed upon their employers. Civil penalties paid by bad bosses will also be funneled back into the Department of Labor to hire more staff and provide resources to workers.

Labor Rights for Incarcerated People Incarcerated workers were considered essential during the pandemic lockdowns but are denied basic workplace protections under the law. I will support legislation that amends the state constitution to prohibit forced labor in New York state prisons, ensure that voluntary labor is fairly compensated, and create a prison labor board to monitor and enforce these changes.

Childcare Workers Childcare is a vital service that requires public investment. Half of all childcare workers in NYC earn wages low enough to qualify for public assistance. The Universal Childcare Act would ensure services are affordable for working families and guarantee childcare workers are paid a living wage.

Building Worker Power In recent years, thousands of workers who were previously thought to be unorganizable — because of the law or because their employers are too powerful — have begun to organize themselves. From Amazon warehouse workers to Starbucks baristas, from delivery drivers to student workers, the “unorganizable” are banding together to win a prosperous future for themselves and their families. I promise to encourage a strong labor movement and stand behind workers who are taking up this fight.

Ending the “Independent Contractor” Scam Companies like Uber, Lyft, and GrubHub exploit their workers by misclassifying them as independent contractors rather than employees. This allows them to ignore labor laws and removes drivers’ legal right to unionize. But under current New York State law, this is legal. I will fight to pass a labor standard that forces gig companies to recognize these workers as employees.

Universal Right to Strike Under New York’s Taylor law, public sector workers face severe penalties for withholding their labor. A universal right to strike would empower all workers — including teachers, sanitation workers and transit workers — to take collective action and create the workplaces they deserve. I also support expanding unemployment insurance for striking workers.

Queer Liberation Queer and trans rights and safety are under attack across the U.S. New York must do more to become a leader in promoting queer liberation, by both addressing these attacks directly and investing in housing and healthcare.

New York has long been a haven for queer people searching for acceptance and community, but it has not always lived up to this promise. As the LGTBQ+ community faces rightwing backlash and restrictions on healthcare and participation in society across much of the United States, it is that much more necessary for New York to step up and be a sanctuary for the queer community.

My vision for District 37 and New York is a community where LGBTQ+ people live authentically without fear and where violence, harassment, and discrimination have no place. To achieve that vision, I will support legislation to preserve access to the healthcare that queer New Yorkers rely on and to make this and all healthcare available to all. I will advocate to preserve and expand the anti-discrimination protections that New Yorkers receive in housing and the workplace.

Pass the New York Equal Rights Amendment, which would prohibit discrimination by the government for all New Yorkers, including discrimination based on a person’s sex, sexual orientation, gender identity, and gender expression. This would protect LGBTQI+ public sector workers, as well as those living in public housing and anyone receiving services from the state.

Pass the full Good Cause Eviction bill so that landlords can’t rely on pretexts in order to evict LGBTQ+ tenants for discriminatory reasons, and provide protections for homeless LGBTQ+ youth, who are disproportionately represented in runaway and homeless youth centers.

Pass the New York Health Act, providing free high-quality healthcare to all New Yorkers, and the 340B Prescription Drug Anti-Discrimination Act to preserve the healthcare many LGBTQ+ New Yorkers rely on.

Develop legislation to expand the ban on conversion therapy to adults under guardianship, so that no New Yorker is forced to suffer cruel attempts to subvert their identity, and provide support for survivors of conversion therapy.

Decriminalize sex work and expunge criminal records. Trans women face especially harsh discrimination without employment protections and often turn to sex work to survive. Until recently, the law didn’t just permit police to target trans women suspected of engaging in sex work—it encouraged them to do so. Decriminalization of sex work acknowledges the lived realities and histories of sex workers, and works towards rectifying past and ongoing injustices.
Develop legislation to confront the abuse and discrimination LGBTQ+ New Yorkers face in jails and prisons while working toward decarceral solutions to public safety issues.

Pass legislation requiring New York schools provide comprehensive, LGBTQ+ inclusive sex education and require schools to establish policies to protect LGBTQ+ students from harassment, bullying, and discrimination. School should be a place of acceptance and discovery for students, not a trauma for them to overcome.

Public Safety Decades of defunding healthcare, housing, libraries, and after-school programs has had devastating results. We need to prevent crime, not just react to it. That means investing in defunded programs proven to create true public safety.

Every New Yorker has a right to feel safe, but for too long we’ve let tabloid sensationalism dictate our public safety priorities, not data and community needs. Together, we can change that. In Albany, I’ll make sure we do everything we can to prevent crime before it happens by addressing the root causes that drive it, not relying on the same failed solutions to respond to it after the fact.

We have the tools to do so. Data shows that crime goes down when people have access to mental health treatment, when their jobs and homes are secure , and when they feel genuinely connected to their community. That should guide our investment in public safety.

Tailored responses to public safety needs We are overburdening the police and legal system, turning to them to address too many problems when we have better options at our disposal. Sending the police to respond to mental health crises, for instance, is inappropriate and can even cause further harm, as it did in the tragic killing of teenager Win Rozario in our own backyard.
Trained crisis responders should have been sent to Rozario, not armed police officers, and we should expand civilian crisis responders across New York.

We should also invest in programs that reduce crime long-term by drawing on the strength of our neighborhoods. Community violence interruption programs rely on relationships between neighbors to drive down crime, and have reduced gun violence by as much as 30 percent in cities across the country. New York should expand them. It should also build community hubs, which are staffed by city employees who provide mental health treatment, job readiness programs, housing assistance, and more.

Meeting Mental Health Needs We should stop relying on jails to handle acute mental health needs. Over half of the people currently held on Rikers Island have a diagnosable mental health condition, and the jail is now the largest mental health institution in the state. That is not only an injustice, it compounds public safety issues down the line by subjecting people who need support to the horrific conditions inside Rikers.

Instead, we should pass the Treatment Not Jail Act, which expands eligibility for mental health and drug court diversion programs for people who need and would benefit from that type of treatment rather than jail.

Treating substance use addiction as a public health need We must also address the drug crisis in our community. Saving lives is the only way of ensuring that individuals have a chance to address their substance use. Since the beginning of the COVID pandemic, overdose deaths in New York have spiked to record levels, with over 6,670 deaths in 2022, and numbers from 2023 will likely be even higher.

To truly reckon with the overdose epidemic, we must address the full spectrum of needs, beginning with preventing problematic substance use. We must also protect the lives and health of those who use drugs through harm reduction measures, ensuring access to treatment for those ready to address their problematic use through support for those in long term recovery. The Treatment Not Jail Act will provide the infrastructure we need for those supports.

These services benefit the whole community, including survivors of crime. The overwhelming majority of victims of crime would rather invest in rehabilitation in prevention than longer sentences. We must listen to them.

Ending Hate Violence No one should ever have to fear for their personal safety because of their race, religion, gender identity, or country of origin. All our struggles for safety are interlinked. Whether it’s white supremacists peddling anti-semitic conspiracies, attacks on the trans community, or the overpolicing of Black and brown communities, I will always stand with those targeted and persecuted.

As a legislator, I will lean on community-based organizations to lead on developing safety plans, use my office to provide educational resources, work with a variety of partners to support survivors of hate, and work to provide restorative opportunities for accountability, healing and growth.

Elder Parole As an assemblymember, I will actively fight to reduce the prison population. Our current system of mass incarceration persists in part because many incarcerated people are sentenced to unimaginably long sentences, without opportunities for release. Fair and timely Parole, and Elder Parole would provide more incarcerated folks, especially elders, with meaningful opportunities to appear before parole boards and have a chance at earlier release.

Require racial impact statements for legislation Black and Latino New Yorkers are dramatically overrepresented in the state’s correctional population. This racially disparate correctional population is unacceptable.

I support the Racial and Ethnic Equity Act that would require an impact statement attached to any legislation that could potentially increase the correctional population; create a new offense; change the penalty for an existing offense; change the existing sentencing, parole or probation procedures; increase the child welfare population; or change social service laws as they relate to access to public assistance.

Transit for All NYC has some of the worst traffic and produces more automobile carbon emissions than any other city in the U.S. We must design our transit system to get more New Yorkers out of cars, reduce carbon emissions, and clean the air.

Every year, hundreds of New Yorkers are killed by cars in crashes, and thousands more are injured. Our transportation system causes a devastating public health crisis that ruins lives and destroys families simply because our streets are designed only around cars. We have many opportunities through legislation and advocacy to make our streets safer and prevent the suffering that traffic violence brings to New Yorkers of all backgrounds.

Transportation policy is directly linked to economic justice, health justice, and environmental justice. If the state makes it easy, fast, and cheap to get across the city by train, bus, bike, or foot — then New Yorkers have better access to jobs, education, childcare, and recreation. Right now, our trains are unreliable, our buses are slow, but fares continue to go up.
A world-class transportation system would give New Yorkers more control over our lives and give us all more agency in the basic choices we make for ourselves and our families.

While NYC has the most expansive public transit system in the country, it also has some of the worst traffic and produces the most carbon emissions from automobile use in the U.S. Particulate pollution from vehicles causes a host of respiratory and cardiovascular problems for New Yorkers. We must design our transit system to get more New Yorkers out of cars, reduce carbon emissions, and clean the air.

A Safe, Reliable, and Efficient Transportation System Free Buses for All Last year, the MTA announced a pilot for five city buses to go fare free. This was a smash hit, leading to ridership increases of up to 20% on those lines. Disgracefully, the 2024 state budget has allowed this pilot to expire, instead of expanding it. The working class New Yorkers who ride buses make this city run and allow the economy of New York City — home to more millionaires than any other city on Earth — to operate.
Our fares are a regressive tax that subsidizes this system. We should be moving towards free fares for all buses (and then trains) and I will advocate fiercely for this as a legislator.

Expand Bus Service Many parts of our district are over half a mile from a subway station. A robust and reliable bus network is our best option to quickly boost our transit system and fill in gaps. I will advocate for expansion of bus service across the city and installation of bus lanes and bus priority signals wherever feasible.

I also believe we need to invest in our express bus system more—with the onset of congestion pricing, some parts of Assembly District 37 far from the subway are now left without an affordable and direct way to get to Midtown and Lower Manhattan. Express buses can fill this gap.

MTA Transparency The MTA pays some of the highest prices in the world on subway construction, while European cities like London and Paris with similarly old subway systems and strong labor protections manage to expand their subways for fractions of the cost. The MTA wastes billions of tax dollars—and New Yorkers’ dreams of an expanded subway system—to consultants and contractors that drive up the cost of capital projects without providing value.
In my role as a legislator, I will fight for a more accountable and transparent MTA that can keep capital costs down so we can enjoy the fruits of subway expansion within our lifetimes.

Lower Montauk Branch Restoration Until 1998, the Long Island Rail Road made stops across Ridgewood, Maspeth, Sunnyside, and Long Island City in areas far from subway stations. The tracks remain and are now lightly used freight rail. In 2018, a study found that over 20,000 riders—many of whom are residents of Assembly District 37 and may disproportionately rely on cars to get around—would ride a restored Lower Montauk Branch on a daily basis.

I support the restoration of this line for passenger service, to reconnect residents across the district to Long Island City, Jamaica, and the rest of the City with a safe and reliable transit option.

Make Citibike Public Bike share has been a welcome addition to our transit landscape since it expanded to many of our neighborhoods in the past few years. It allows many New Yorkers to easily make short trips and connect to other forms of transit.

However, it is getting unreasonably expensive – annual memberships have gone up over 100% since the launch of the system 10 years ago and it now costs almost $5 to take a bike out for 30 minutes if you don’t pay yearly. This is because it is contracted out to a multinational company (Lyft) to run at a profit, and not as a public service like the rest of the city’s transit services.
It is past time for the city to run our public bike share system like a public transportation system to keep fees low and keep the system reliable for all communities that it serves.

End Traffic Violence Fight for Street Safety Improvements As your Assembly Member, I will use my office to organize and advocate for the NYC Department of Transportation to implement safety projects that protect pedestrians and cyclists on dangerous corridors and intersections across the district. DOT has a wide array of designs and interventions that are proven to save lives: protected bike lanes, curb extensions, pedestrian medians, signal timing changes, scramble crosswalks, daylighting, and more.

It is especially time for a safe bike network in Ridgewood and a safe bike route that connects Ridgewood to Sunnyside. DOT often responds to pressure from elected officials to pursue these designs, and I will amplify community demands for these interventions.

Automate Traffic Enforcement The speed camera program in NYC has been successful in reducing speeding where they are deployed. They also have the potential to remove the NYPD from traffic enforcement: reducing opportunities for traffic stops that can escalate dangerously, and reducing reliance on irregular and biased enforcement. I would support legislation to expand the city’s speed camera program to promote safe driving and pedestrian safety across the city.

Regulate Heavy Vehicles With each passing year, passenger cars and trucks in the U.S. are getting bigger and the implications on pedestrians and cyclists are increasingly deadly. Giant SUVs and pickup trucks are not designed for use on local NYC streets with heavy pedestrian traffic. I support legislation currently proposed that would increase state registration fees for heavier vehicles in an attempt to discourage their purchase in New York.

Assemblymember Marcela Mitaynes Assembly District 51 Biography Assemblymember Marcela Mitaynes represents Red Hook, Sunset Park and northern Bay Ridge. Marcela migrated to New York City from Peru as a child with her family and was raised in Sunset Park, Brooklyn. She is now raising her own family in that same vibrant, beautiful community.

Marcela attended elementary school at P.S. 169 in Sunset Park. Her daughter went on to go to the same elementary school and Marcela served as president of the PTA at P.S. 169. She has also proven to be an active member of her community as a member of Community Board 7 for 10 years.

Marcela was evicted from her rent-stabilized apartment of 30 years, and began her life’s work of empowering her neighbors to know their rights and find their voices to fight to stay in their homes. Through her work with Neighbors Helping Neighbors, and with tenants throughout New York State, Marcela was instrumental in the passage of the historic Housing Stability and Tenant Protection Act of 2019.
This legislation dramatically and comprehensively strengthened the rights of tenants in rent-stabilized apartments to defend their homes and communities.

Marcela is continuing to organize in the district and help build power for working class people. All New Yorkers deserve access to housing, health care and energy. We need to build a mass, working-class movement to win a future where working-class people have a chance to live dignified lives.

Skip navigation menu Our Campaign's Top Issues The problems we face aren't mysterious. They're the result of systems that have been rewritten over time to serve the few at the expense of everyone else. These are my positions — not a list of talking points, but a reflection of how I actually think about what needs to change and why.

My Progressive Commitments I am a progressive Democrat and plan to seek membership in the Congressional Progressive Caucus if elected. I wholeheartedly adopt the Progressive Promise, which is the CPC's platform built on advancing justice, dignity, and peace for all people, tackling systems of oppression, demanding a government and economy that works for people over the wealthy and powerful, and a commitment to sweeping, transformative change.
Read the full Progressive Promise here. Democratic Reform Affordability and Economic Justice Workers, Labor, and Employees The Central Coast and Environment
Human Rights Rights, Freedom, and Privacy Fiduciary Responsibility Monopoly and Market Power Technology, Crypto, and AI Education, Media Literacy, and Civic Life

Immigration and Federal Agency Reform Incarceration and Criminal Justice National Security and Diplomacy Constituent Services Democratic Reform Democracy only works when institutions answer to the people. Right now, sadly they do not. That's not an accident. Congress is named first in the Constitution, but over the years, Congress has delegated much of its power to the executive branch. Decades of concentrated money and influence has resulted in consolidated power. Addressing this is my absolute top priority, because fixing this is the prerequisite for fixing everything else.

Affordability and Economic Justice Life, especially here on the Central Coast, is increasingly expensive. My parents bought a modest home in Ventura on a teacher and a car salesman's salary in the 1980s. That life is out of reach for working families now. It's out of reach for me as a renter. These are policy failures that must be corrected.

Workers, Labor, and Employees Work should provide dignity, security, together with a fair share of what you help create. This includes protection from exploitation and retaliation, access to affordable healthcare, and the ability to live on what you earn without needing multiple jobs. This isn’t a radical notion. It’s the American Dream, and it’s one we all deserve to wake up to.

The Central Coast and Environment I’m watching people get priced out of the place that raised them. Housing costs and environmental risk are reshaping our communities, our coastline, our forests, and our way of life. Climate change isn’t a future problem here. We need to protect what makes our home livable, and make sure the people who live and work here can stay.

Human Rights I believe in human rights as a governing principle. I believe in having the moral clarity to take an immediate stand for human rights when others are in violation, even when the perpetrator is an ally. We must apply standards consistently and hold everyone accountable, including our allies and including ourselves. I support a ceasefire in Palestine, an end to the war in Iran, humanitarian access, and a broader shift toward restraint, diplomacy, and a recommitment to international law.

I support the UN Universal Declaration of Human Rights and belive the U.S. should reaffirm it at home. Our foreign policy should reflect our core American values – life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness.

Rights, Freedom, and Privacy Everyone deserves the right to lead their life on their own terms. Dignity, autonomy, and freedom from manipulation. From digital privacy to civil rights, bodily autonomy to religious freedom for all. This is the foundation of what it means to live in a free society.

Fiduciary Responsibility Budgets are value statements. The federal budget should reflect the priorities of the American people, not defense contractors, foreign agents, or oligarchs. Congress has a fiduciary duty to spend responsibly and invest in people. We also need to rein in unsustainable debt and rising interest costs.

Monopoly and Market Power America is not a free market. Across all industries – healthcare, housing, food, tech, finance – consolidation is driving up prices and concentrating power in fewer hands. Competition is healthy. Remember that we are serving people first, not the few leaders at the top of corporate conglomerates. We must enforce antitrust law, put a check on private equity in essential industries, rebuild regulatory capacity, and protect small businesses and workers from predatory practices.

Technology, Crypto, and AI Technology has reshaped who hold power. Right now that power is concentrated and largely unregulated. Tech moves fast, government does not. We need congressional leaders who understand the tech industry and are willing to act quickly. Congress needs to take the lead on accountability for AI, serious regulation of crypto to prevent fraud and systemic risk, oversight of the technology industry in general, and breaking up monopolistic platforms.
Innovation in the tech industry has driven America’s economic strength; however, technology should serve people, not the other way around.

Education, Media Literacy, and Civic Life A well-informed citizenry is necessary for a healthy democracy. Our Constitution calls for a well-regulated militia but misses the mark in failing to call for a well-educated public. We must invest in public education at every level and treat civic literacy, arts, and humanities as essential. We are also living in a crisis of misinformation and manipulation. I support a modernized Fairness Doctrine for the 21st century.

Immigration and Federal Agency Reform Our immigration system is broken in ways that hurt real people in our area every single day. I won’t mince words – I support abolishing ICE and fundamentally reforming the Department of Homeland Security. The agencies and individuals responsible for enforcement have become unaccountable. Immigration enforcement needs reform.

Incarceration and Criminal Justice Mass incarceration has failed. Our carceral system functions in many ways as modern-day slavery. It fails to make communities safer, doesn’t deliver justice to victims, and disproportionately targets Black and brown communities. I oppose for-profit prisons and support reform of a carceral system focused on accountability, restorative justice, rehabilitation, reentry, and addressing root causes like mental health and substance use.

National Security and Diplomacy Military dominance alone isn’t security. Intervention doesn’t keep us safe. America is safer with strong relationships. We spend more on defense than the next several countries combined, yet undervalue the power of strong diplomatic relations, dialogue, and deterrence. The current administration’s slogan is “Peace through Strength”. Let’s re-define strength to focus on the strength of our relationships, respect, and mutual understanding with those around the globe.
I support renewed American participation in the United Nations as well as a number of reforms to strengthen international cooperation across the many international organizations.

Constituent Services Your representative works for you and all of CA-24 which includes Santa Barbara, San Luis Obispo, and Ventura counties. This is representation in both directions: helping people access federal services and understand policy, and making sure that our communities and our many voices are heard in Washington. I will invest in strong, accessible constituent services offices across the district.

← All issues Public Safety policy details Background Safety isn't a talking point. It's a promise you make to the people in your life — your students, your neighbors, your kids. Lauren has spent 17 years in classrooms and knows what it feels like to run an active shooter drill with 10-year olds and pretend it's normal. It shouldn't be normal. And in Louisiana’s 1st District, on too many issues that touch our safety, the people we send to Washington have stopped showing up for us.

Gun Violence Prevention Steve Scalise has an A+ rating from the NRA. He survived being shot on a baseball field in 2017. Yet months later, he led House Republican opposition to the Bipartisan Safer Communities Act, the first major federal gun safety law in nearly 30 years. That bill funded crisis intervention, closed the "boyfriend loophole" for domestic abusers, and strengthened background checks for buyers under 21. He called it an attack on the Second Amendment. It passed anyway, with 14 Republican votes. His vote wasn't one of them.

And the numbers back up why that fight mattered. Louisiana has the second-highest rate of gun deaths in the country, just behind Mississippi. Nearly 1,300 people died from gun-related injuries here in 2023 alone. Firearms are the leading cause of death for Louisiana kids ages 1 to 17, and our child gun death rate is close to three times the national average.

As a teacher, Lauren has experienced this personally, losing several students to gun violence during her career. And unlike the rest of the country, where gun suicide makes up the majority of gun deaths, in Louisiana the majority are homicides. This isn't primarily a mental health story, it's a community violence story.

The trend is getting worse, not better: gun deaths in Louisiana rose 49% from 2014 to 2023, and gun homicides rose a staggering 86%, both far outpacing the national increase. In 2024, the state repealed its concealed carry permit requirement, meaning you can now carry a loaded gun in public with no background check and no training. Our gun law ranking dropped from 26th to 33rd in the country as a result.
Lauren is not interested in taking anyone's guns. She is interested in keeping them out of the wrong hands. Those are different things, and Louisiana voters know the difference.

Community violence Real public safety isn't just about the moment a crime happens. It's about everything upstream of it including mental health care, youth programs, quality and stability in our schools, strong public infrastructure, economic opportunity, and law enforcement that has the staffing and training to do its job well. Cutting those investments doesn't make us safer. It just moves the cost somewhere else, usually onto emergency rooms and jails.

Over-policing and overcriminalization Louisiana locks up more of its people, per capita, than any democracy on earth and we have an incarceration rate of roughly 1,067 per 100,000 residents. This is a distinction the state has held for decades. Louisiana's own bipartisan Justice Reinvestment Task Force looked at the numbers and found the honest answer: it isn't because Louisiana has more violent crime than its neighbors.

It's because Louisiana sends people to prison for nonviolent offenses — drug possession most of all — far more often than almost anywhere else. That's not public safety. That's a policy choice, and it's an expensive, generational one that falls hardest on Black communities, who make up about a third of Louisiana's population but roughly two-thirds of the people behind bars.

And right here in Louisiana’s 1st District, we've seen where unchecked surveillance leads. Jefferson Parish sheriff's deputies once arrested and jailed a man named Randal Reid for days for crimes he didn't commit because facial recognition software wrongly flagged him as a match even though he had never even been to Louisiana. The Sheriff's Office later settled the lawsuit. That's what happens when departments lean on unproven, racially biased technology instead of real investigative work.

In New Orleans, police were caught running real-time facial recognition surveillance in violation of the city's own ordinance. This was done quietly, for years, without telling the public they were doing it. Watching everyone doesn't make anyone safer. It erodes the trust that actually keeps communities and police working together, and it's communities of color who pay the price first.

← All issues Defend Social Security policy details Background The crisis of Social Security is looming. Social Security is the promise this country made to every worker: pay in your whole life, and you'll have something to retire on. That promise is now on a clock because the trust fund is projected to run dry by the end of 2032, triggering an automatic 22% benefit cut unless Congress acts. In fact, it's a district full of retirees or people nearing retirement, and a 22% cut would hit a senior in Terrebonne or Lafourche just as hard whether they worked a rig, a classroom, or a shrimp boat. Social Security is what many families in our district rely on as their primary source of retirement income. Congress keeps kicking the can down the road instead of acting while the fix is still manageable.

← All issues Quality Healthcare is a Human Right for Every Community policy details Background Lauren believes that healthcare is not a luxury. It is not a privilege for the well-connected. It is a human right. Every family in this district and country deserves care they can easily access and care that won't bankrupt them to receive.

We are in the middle of a doctor shortage. Nearly half our neighbors are on Medicaid or have no insurance at all. With a median age of 39.9 in Louisiana’s 1st Congressional District, a significant portion of our population relies on Medicare, Social Security, and Medicaid to cover healthcare and basic needs. It doesn't stop there. Too many families have no dental coverage, no vision coverage, and no access to mental health care.
Our rural hospitals are disappearing. More than 30 rural hospitals in Louisiana are at risk of closing their doors because Washington keeps cutting the funding that keeps them open.

When it comes to women's health, the crisis is even deeper. Louisiana has some of the highest maternal mortality rates in the country. We don't have enough OB/GYNs. We have maternity care deserts. And Black mothers in this state are dying at rates no family should ever have to accept. Lauren believes that high quality healthcare includes reproductive justice and bodily autonomy.

Our veterans are caught in this crisis too. Louisiana is home to tens of thousands of veterans, many in rural parishes where the nearest VA facility is hours away. When rural hospitals close, veterans lose the community care options they depend on. They served this country and they shouldn't have to fight another battle just to see a doctor.

For millions of seniors and people with disabilities, Medicaid's promise isn't just coverage. It means the ability to stay in their own home or near their own family instead of being sent to a nursing home or institution. That's what Home and Community-Based Services (HCBS) makes possible.

However, while Medicaid is required to cover nursing home care, HCBS is still classified as an "optional" benefit and one that states can scale back whenever budgets get tight or the political winds shift. That gap has always been a vulnerability. Now it's being tested directly. In June 2026, the Department of Justice issued new guidance signaling the administration may not enforce the community-integration mandate established by the Supreme Court's landmark Olmstead decision.

That decision comes as HCBS is already under strain nationwide, following the largest Medicaid cuts in the program's history. The message this sends is unmistakable: the guardrails that kept disabled and aging Americans out of institutions are loosening, right as the safety net underneath them is being cut.

Lauren knows what's at stake here personally, through her own family's experience with disability advocacy, and as a special education teacher who has spent 17 years fighting for the dignity and independence of the students and families she has served.

← All issues Protect the Right to Vote policy details Background For a century after Reconstruction, Louisiana and its neighboring states built an entire system to keep people from voting: poll taxes, literacy tests, grandfather clauses, and outright violence and intimidation, all aimed at Black voters and anyone else who threatened the political order. It took the civil rights movement to force passage of the Voting Rights Act of 1965, which finally put federal teeth behind the promise that every citizen gets a say.

That history is not abstract here. To Lauren, growing up in a town not far from Seneca Falls, New York and the origin of the women’s suffrage movement taught her something from an early age: the right to vote has never been handed to anyone in this country. It's been fought for, generation after generation, against people determined to deny it or take it away.

Today, the tactics have changed, but the goal hasn't. Voting rights are under attack, both in Washington and right here at home. Steve Scalise personally championed the SAVE America Act, a law that requires documentary proof of citizenship just to register to vote and photo ID at the polls. This isn't election security.

It's a solution in search of a problem, and the real effect falls on eligible citizens especially seniors, rural voters, the disabled, working families, and married women who don't have easy access to a passport or certified birth certificate.

Here in Louisiana, we watched our own primary get delayed and our congressional maps redrawn behind closed doors after the Supreme Court's ruling in Louisiana v. Callais. This has left voters confused about their own district in the middle of an election cycle.

Whether it's a literacy test in 1955, a redrawn map in Baton Rouge in 2026, or a new documentary-proof requirement in Washington, the pattern is the same: when the people in power are worried about who might vote them out, they make it harder to vote at all.
We don't have to accept that. This district has always been worth fighting for. So is every voter's right to be heard.

← All issues Promote Clean Energy, Protect Our Coast and Environment policy details Background Louisiana is popularly known as the “Sportsman’s Paradise,” but our swamps, wetlands, coast, breathing air, farmlands, housing properties, and way of life have become a toxic dumping ground for billionaires and corporations, with their significant PAC contributions to politicians like Steve Scalise. Steve Scalise has taken more than $2.1 million from the fossil fuel industry over his career. This is the second-most of any member of the U.S. House.

In just the 2023-24 cycle alone, he ranked fourth among all House lawmakers in oil and gas contributions, including $40,000 from the PAC of an oil executive later accused by federal regulators of colluding with OPEC to keep gas prices artificially high.

Louisiana needs a representative who treats coastal and environmental survival as a long-term, bipartisan infrastructure priority rather than a side effect of energy policy, and not something to defend only when the money's flowing in.

COASTAL EROSION Louisiana is losing its coast in real time. Every hour, the state loses roughly a football field of wetlands and every year since the 1930s, Louisiana loses about 25-35 square miles of wetlands which is an area similar to the size of Delaware. This is land that protects communities from storm surge, sustains the fishing and shrimping industries that built this district, and keeps saltwater out of drinking water supplies.

Coastal communities like Isle de Jean Charles have already been forced to relocate as the land beneath them disappears. Additionally, communities in Jefferson, Orleans, Plaquemines, St. Bernard, and Terrebonne parishes face rising flood risks, with some areas expecting up to 2 feet of sea level rise by 2050.

Our state receives real money for coastal restoration through GOMESA: offshore drilling revenue sharing has funded wetland restoration and flood protection. That funding matters, and this district should keep using every dollar of it well.

However, that same revenue stream ties Louisiana's coastal survival to the continued expansion of the very industry accelerating the crisis — deeper drilling, more leases, more emissions — without a serious federal plan for what happens when the oil runs out or the climate makes today's coastline unrecognizable. Our state remains dependent on the same industry driving the crisis we collectively face.

Even as drilling revenue has increased, the broader federal commitment to coastal resilience has been cut. In the Fiscal Year 2026 federal budget, NOAA eliminated Coastal Zone Management Grants (-$81.5 million), eliminated National Coastal Resilience Funds (-$32 million), eliminated the National Estuarine Research Reserve System (-$33.3 million), and terminated the Habitat Conservation & Restoration Program (-$56.2 million). This was alongside roughly $280 million in rescinded NOAA climate resilience funds.
These are exactly the programs that fund the science, monitoring, and habitat restoration work that drilling revenue alone can't replace.

AI & HYPERSCALE DATA CENTERS Louisiana is becoming a national hub for hyperscale data center construction, and it's happening fast. Meta's Hyperion data center in Richland Parish has grown from an initial $10 billion project to a $50 billion, 5-gigawatt facility. This is one of the largest AI infrastructure investments in the world. To power it, Entergy is building 10 new power plants across three parishes, including new gas-fired generation.
Meta's data center could use around six times more power than the entire city of New Orleans on one of the hottest days of the year.

This kind of investment can mean temporary jobs and community investment, but none of those advantages should come at the expense of people’s safety or professional livelihoods. Working class people and families in America deserve innovation that works with them, not against them. Congress must use its power to conduct research, pass legislation, and create regulations ensuring artificial intelligence methods and technologies are used in ways that are ethical, responsible, transparent, and regulated.

CARBON CAPTURE STORAGE (CCS) Louisiana is at the center of many of the largest carbon capture and storage (CCS) projects in the country and world. There are currently dozens of Class VI carbon injection well applications across nearly 20 Louisiana parishes. Many Louisiana residents have expressed concern that the CCS projects will affect our health, wildlife, lakes, water systems, agricultural industry, tourism, and constitutional property rights.

Carbon capture projects also generate their own emissions. They are one of the most expensive emissions reduction measures and require government subsidies to be economically viable. These projects often come at the cost of landowners' rights and public safety. Too often, the companies proposing these projects have kept basic details and overall impacts undisclosed, leaving the people living above these pipelines and injection sites in the dark about risks to their land, water, and air.

For most individuals or families, buying a home is the biggest financial decision they'll ever make and in Louisiana, that decision has gotten harder every year. Lauren knows this firsthand. She bought her home here in Louisiana, and remembers what it took to make that leap — the savings, the paperwork, the fear of one unexpected cost throwing the whole plan off, and the ongoing maintenance of home ownership. That experience shapes how she thinks about this issue, because it's not abstract to her. It's personal.

Louisiana homeowners are still experiencing a property insurance crisis that Louisiana's own Insurance Commissioner describes as ongoing, even as the market slowly improves. Realtors across the state of Louisiana often report of deals collapsing at the closing table when buyers discover what it will cost to insure the home behind the mortgage they've already qualified forThis means families who can afford a mortgage are still being priced out by the cost of insuring the home behind it.

Rising premiums have made the affordable housing shortage in Louisiana's metro areas worse and has taken a toll on the housing market across south Louisiana. The historical effects of redlining are still seen in New Orleans and the district’s surrounding parishes today, contributing to cycles of poverty.

Lauren believes that housing is a human right and that a strong community starts with people being able to afford to live in it. ← All issues Good Jobs and Benefits, Modern Economy policy details Background Louisiana workers are being left behind. In Jefferson Parish alone, the living wage for a single adult is estimated at roughly $22 an hour, a gap of nearly $15 an hour between what the law requires and what it actually takes to make ends meet. A full-time worker earning minimum wage in this district brings home about $15,000 a year. This is below the poverty line for a family of two.

Lauren has spent her career organizing alongside members of her teacher’s union, and she knows what it's like to watch her union brothers and sisters in a “right to work” state fight hard to negotiate contracts that win safe working conditions and strong benefits. It closes the loopholes that let employers drag out union elections and retaliate against workers for organizing. Workers must have a real say in our pay and our safety. Scalise has sided with the employers every time. Lauren won't.

This district doesn't need more corporate tax breaks that never trickle down. And it doesn’t need cuts to benefits that were long promised. It needs a representative who has stood in a classroom, not a boardroom and who understands that a modern economy has to work for the people building it, not just the shareholders profiting from it.

As a member and leader within her teacher’s union and someone who has stood on picket lines in solidarity with fellow unions, Lauren understands that we must build a future in which all people in Louisiana and the United States have access to good-paying, fulfilling jobs that allow them to thrive, not just survive.

For fifty years, Congress promised to cover 40% of the cost of educating students with disabilities. Today, the federal share is under 12 percent — leaving states like Louisiana to make up the difference, or make cuts. Additionally, as our federal administration has pushed to dismantle the Department of Education and move these programs to the Department of Health and Human Services, they're stripping away the oversight that makes IDEA protections real and not just promises on paper.
Gutting the Department doesn't shrink government waste. It removes the one watchdog making sure schools follow the law for the kids who need it most.

These failures don't stay in Washington. They land on teachers, and on the students who need the most support and get the least. In states like Louisiana, where they only get a fraction of the special education funding it is owed, this is devastating. Louisiana's schools still rank among the bottom 15 states nationally. Nearly one in six students don't graduate high school.
Teachers here have worked hard to ensure students make gains in reading and math, but earn about $56,000, well below the national average, all while school funding has stagnated.

Nationally, teacher pay has stagnated for a decade while the cost of living escalates. Special education classrooms are short-staffed. Funding formulas built decades ago haven't caught up to what students need today. This is especially true for students with disabilities, our multilingual learners, and students facing adverse childhood experiences such as trauma and poverty.

Instead of investing in our schools and the public good of public education, politicians and billionaires are attacking the people who teach and learn in them. Teachers are being vilified for teaching honest history and real civics which are the very subjects that build informed citizens. Cuts to school meal programs mean kids go hungry during the school day and are unable to focus and learn because Washington decided a lunch tray was expendable.

Grant funding for arts and music education programs are constantly at the whim of congressional and departmental budget cycles. All of these things make it difficult for teachers to do their jobs and harder for kids to learn.

Lauren knows that ensuring a quality education for kids with disabilities uplifts all kids. She knows it will take a member of Congress who has hands-on experience in our schools to fight for the investment our students were promised fifty years ago, support teachers and school staff instead of scapegoating them, and make sure our schools teach students the literacy, social, technology, and critical thinking skills needed to take on our evolving world.

Lauren’s K-12 Priorities in Congress Fight to fully fund federal special education law (IDEA- Individuals with Disabilities Education Act) and fight just as hard to keep it where it belongs, at the Department of Education, not scattered across agencies with no expertise in how students with disabilities learn
Cosponsor federal measures to raise the teacher pay floor to pay teachers what they’re worth and end the decade-long stagnation that's driving educators out of the classroom
Invest in both job training and college prep so students have multiple paths to success Protect and expand Title II funding for educator recruitment, retention, and training

Fight for increased Title I funding to close the resource gap for schools serving students in low-income communities Oppose billionaire backed voucher and educational savings account schemes that jeopardize public school funding
Push to restore and protect NEA, NEH, and IMLS grants that keep music, art, and cultural programs in schools and communities
Defend the right of educators to teach honest history and real civics, free from political interference because informed citizens start with an honest education
Establish universal pre-kindergarten programs for all 3 and 4 year olds and ensure we have strong Head Start and Early Steps programs
Support our multilingual learners by advocating for funding for ELL programs, certified staff, and resources for immigrant and refugee students

Higher Education Background The failure doesn't end at graduation. The same Congress that's underfunding K-12 and attacking teachers is making college less affordable on the other end. They’re raising the cost of borrowing, taxing loan forgiveness as income, and causing a shortfall in the Pell Grant program that could leave students without aid in just a few years.

A student who makes it through our K-12 system in schools in Louisiana and in states across the country shouldn't graduate into a higher education system where the challenges are already stacked against them.

Higher education is becoming more out of reach, not less. The "One Big Beautiful Bill Act" raised the cost of borrowing for Louisiana students and caps graduate student loans at $20,500 per year with a $100,000 lifetime limit. Starting in 2026, any forgiven student debt is taxable. Repayment plans are being consolidated into a system where borrowers can be locked into payments for up to 30 years.

Meanwhile, the program millions of Louisiana students rely on to even get to college is running out of money. The Pell Grant program is projected to face a cumulative 10-year shortfall exceeding $100 billion, and without congressional action, could see a disruption in full awards as soon as the 2028-2029 school year.
Lauren’s Higher Education Priorities in Congress Fight to fully fund the Pell Grant program and close the shortfall before it cuts off aid to the students who need it most.
Oppose taxing forgiven student debt as income because this is a policy that punishes borrowers for getting relief they earned.

Protect and strengthen Public Service Loan Forgiveness for jobs like teachers, nurses, social workers, and first responders Cosponsor legislation to lower interest rates on federal student loans and restore reasonable repayment timelines
Expand access to trade, technical, and community college pathways Support debt-free community college and technical training so a two-year degree or certification doesn't start with debt

When we look at foreign policy, the same logic applies. True national security is not just about military strength. It is about fostering global stability through diplomacy such as investments in human infrastructure, specifically education, healthcare, and sustainable development.

Just as a chaotic environment hinders a student's ability to learn, global instability, poverty, hunger, and systemic inequality threaten our safety at home. Moreover, Lauren views issues of war through a disability justice lens, and sees how international conflict can deepen harm and trauma for disabled individuals.

As a country, we must lead in protecting civilians from disasters of war, ethnic and religious hatred, and human rights abuses and aim to engage in international relations that prioritizes diplomacy and everyone’s human rights.

← All issues Support Local Agriculture and Seafood policy details Background

Louisiana’s 1st Congressional District isn't just suburbs and city blocks. It's strawberry fields in Tangipahoa. It's dairy farms that have fed Florida Parishes families for generations. It's shrimp boats out of St. Bernard, Lafourche, and Terrebonne, oyster beds off Plaquemines, and crawfish ponds that show up on tables from Hammond to the French Quarter. Louisiana produces 25% of the nation's seafood and 90% of U.S. crawfish, with an industry worth over $2.4 billion annually. These local economies are under real strain, and Washington keeps failing to show up for it.

Our shrimpers are being squeezed from every direction. The U.S. imports the vast majority of the shrimp it eats, much of it farmed cheaply overseas under conditions that would never meet American environmental or food-safety standards, and it's flooding the market and driving prices down.

On top of that, a February 2026 oil spill from the Louisiana Offshore Oil Port near Port Fourchon forced Wildlife and Fisheries to shut down oyster beds in Terrebonne, leaving oystermen, crabbers, and shrimpers in limbo over how much of their catch and equipment was compromised and whether customers would trust Louisiana seafood again even after the beds reopened.

Our crawfish industry nearly lost a season to visa chaos. Crawfish processing depends heavily on seasonal guest workers who come back year after year to peel and pack the catch. This is work that plants say they cannot find enough local labor to fill. In 2026, federal delays in releasing H-2B visas meant most of the state's crawfish peeling plants started the season with few or none of their usual workers.

Louisiana's agriculture commissioner put the potential economic hit at up to $300 million. This wasn't a natural disaster. It was a paperwork and policy failure in Washington, and it happened right in the middle of peak season, when there was no way to make up for lost time.

Many of our local family farms are struggling or down-sizing operations. Tangipahoa Parish was once home to a huge share of Louisiana's dairy industry, but today there are only a handful of dairy farms left statewide who are competing with giant corporate operations and the rising cost of doing business small. Multi-generational strawberry growers around Ponchatoula and Hammond are fighting rising labor and input costs, extreme weather swings, and shrinking acreage every season.
All of this is happening while the Farm Bill that sets the rules for crop insurance, disaster assistance, and rural investment has been stuck in historic gridlock in Washington, D.C. for years.

Decriminalization of hemp agricultural products. Steve Scalise voted (HR 5371) to prohibit the processing, sale, or use of hemp. While Louisiana does not have a robust hemp farming industry (less than 40 acres of planted farms), it does have a booming hemp beverage and product industry. Our hemp products industry generated $33 million in sales and $4.3 million in tax revenues in Louisiana. This industry employs Louisiana citizens with good paying jobs and is at risk of closing because of Steve Scalise.

Lauren’s Priorities in Congress Invest in agricultural research and marketing to preserve Louisiana’s traditional industries and way of life and recognize that our seafood economy is not just an industry but generations of families and coastal communities

Fight for truth in seafood labeling and ensuring consumers know what they're eating and where it came from Require that producers who are importing seafood here meet the same labor and environmental standards that our fisherman in America have to meet

This includes protecting the wage floor for every individual working within the seafood industry, accountability and enforcement mechanisms so workers can report wage theft or unsafe working conditions without fear of retaliation or deportation, and offering pathways to citizenship for workers who keep these industries running.
