← All issues Infrastructure That Works for Everyone policy details Background Infrastructure isn't an abstract policy category — it's the roads your kids ride the bus on, the bridge you cross to get to work, the ports that bring in goods we purchase and consume, and the water that comes out of your tap. When Lauren bought her home here in Louisiana, she learned quickly that surrounding infrastructure is a key factor, from the road conditions on your street to whether your water and drainage systems can handle the next big storm.
Every person or family that buys a home or moves into this district is making that same bet on their community holding up.

Roads, Bridges, and Ports Right now, that bet is a shaky one. Even though Louisiana's roads, bridges, and ports are the backbone of our economy, many are outdated, congested, and in urgent need of repair. Louisiana's infrastructure currently earns a C- grade from the American Society of Civil Engineers. This is an improvement from a D+ in 2017, but still far from where it needs to be, with six of ten infrastructure categories earning the same or lower grades than eight years ago.

More than 1,500 of Louisiana's bridges are in poor condition, including the Pearl River Bridge on Highway 90 in St. Tammany Parish. This bridge has been closed indefinitely since May 2022 because of structural steel deterioration causing unsafe and inefficient travel for people in District 1.

Even where federal investment has flowed in, it hasn't kept pace with inflation or the state's growing needs. This leaves real funding gaps that prevent Louisiana from addressing its most critical problems. With 12,915 bridges and billions in highway projects underway through the TIMED program, the need for maintenance and upgrades has never been greater. Traffic on I-10 is expected to grow 30% by 2032, making improvements critical for families and commuters across our region.

Broadband Broadband is its own crisis in this district: over 10% of Louisianans live in areas with no broadband infrastructure at all under the FCC's benchmark, and nearly 1 in 5 Louisiana households don't have an internet subscription even where service exists. This is often because it's simply too expensive. In 2026, that's not a minor inconvenience.
It's the difference between a kid finishing homework and a small business staying online, between a rural family reaching a telehealth appointment and going without care.

Clean Water Saltwater is creeping into our drinking water. In 2023, drought dropped the Mississippi River so low that Gulf saltwater pushed upstream toward New Orleans. Plaquemines Parish was hit first. Nearly 2,000 residents went months on bottled water. Some families reported skin rashes from bathing in it. Local businesses lost equipment to corrosion. At its worst, the water tested six and a half times saltier than the EPA's safety threshold.

The Army Corps had to barge in freshwater and race to build an underwater levee before the wedge reached New Orleans, Jefferson, and St. Bernard. This is what happens when drought, sea-level rise, and coastal land loss combine. It will happen again, and next time it could reach more of our district.

Our pipes are old, and it shows. Boil water advisories aren't rare in LA-01. In fact, they're routine. Jefferson Parish has lost water pressure from mains that trace back to the 1940s. St. Tammany has had multiple advisories in a single year from chlorination failures and main breaks. Every time this happens, parents have to boil water before making a baby's bottle, restaurants have to close, and schools have to cancel classes and send kids home.
As a teacher, Lauren experienced this many times and this led to disruptions in learning. That's not a minor inconvenience. It's a sign our water systems are being patched instead of rebuilt.

Lauren’s Priorities in Congress Fight for Louisiana's fair share of federal highway, bridge, and infrastructure formula funding, and ensure it's actually spent on the roads, interstate highways, and bridges rated in poor condition like the Pearl River Bridge on Highway 90 and those used as part of evacuation routes, rather than delayed by political gridlock.
Support the Bridge Investment Program and similar federal funding streams to accelerate repair of Louisiana's highest-risk bridges before they fail, not after.
Expand broadband infrastructure funding specifically targeted at unserved rural parishes in LA-01, and push for subsidies that make existing broadband actually affordable for working families.

Fight for federal infrastructure dollars to invest in resilient water, sewer, and drainage systems so communities aren't left with boil-water advisories and flooded streets every time a storm comes through.

Protect our water supply from saltwater intrusion by supporting coastal restoration projects, pushing for early warning and rapid response systems for affected parishes, and securing permanent and continuous federal funding for the Mississippi River sill system
With community input and approval, protect and modernize port and waterway infrastructure funding critical to Louisiana's maritime and shipping economy.

Require that federal infrastructure dollars come with strong labor standards such as good wages, safety protections, and local-hire requirements so the workers building this infrastructure share in its benefits.

← All issues Immigration policy details Background Immigration policy isn't an abstract debate in Louisiana. Louisiana has become the second-largest center for immigration detention in the United States. After Texas, Louisiana has the most number of people detained in the country, currently detaining 13% of immigrants nationwide.

Our communities have watched immigration enforcement carried out in ways that violate due process and cause families and neighbors to live in fear. ICE has engaged in systemic abuses, including racial profiling, family separation, and the targeting of our immigrant neighbors, and even U.S. citizens, which have undermined the values of justice, dignity, and equality that this nation professes to uphold. Lauren has stood with families in this district dealing with uncertainty connected to enforcement actions.

As a teacher, Lauren has spent her career watching what instability does to kids. When a parent is detained without warning or when a family doesn't know if they'll be together at dinner, a child cannot learn and a community cannot thrive. She has organized with her fellow union members to ensure that immigrant families get connected to the resources and support during the times they need them the most.

And this district owes immigrants something we don't say out loud often enough: gratitude. After Hurricane Katrina, when over 214,000 homes across New Orleans were damaged or destroyed and much of the region lay in ruins, it was immigrant workers who did the grueling, dangerous work of gutting flooded houses, framing new walls, and putting blue tarps over damaged roofs so families could come home.

Nearly half the reconstruction workforce in the months after the storm was Latino, and researchers have found more than half of those workers were undocumented. They worked long days in hazardous conditions, often without protective equipment, and too many were never paid what they were owed. Twenty years later, many of those same workers and their families have put down roots here. They have opened businesses, raised kids in our schools, and become part of the fabric of Southeast Louisiana.

The Hispanic population in the greater New Orleans area has grown substantially since Katrina, adding to our workforce, our tax base, and our local economy. As a state that lives at the mercy of hurricanes and coastal erosion, we know exactly who shows up after the storm. It's long past time that we said thank you and treated these neighbors like the essential part of our recovery and our future that they are.

Congressman Scalise has held this seat for over two decades. In that time, Congress has not passed a single major bipartisan immigration reform bill. Meanwhile, the crises pile up: worker shortages, backlogged courts, and a patchwork of executive actions that swing wildly from one administration to the next because Congress refuses to legislate. LA-01 deserves a representative who will actually do the job.

Lauren’s Priorities in Congress Support the creation of new humane, accountable, and community-centered structures that uphold immigrant rights, prioritizing pathways to citizenship, community safety, and fair labor standards

Advocate for policies that respect immigrants' dignity and refocus federal enforcement on actual public safety threats — not sweeps that destabilize schools, places of worship, workplaces, and neighborhoods
Support a permanent legislative fix for Dreamers who were brought to this country as children and have built their lives here

Push for full independent investigations and oversight when ICE’s actions result in due process violations, injury, or death like in the cases of Keith Porter, Jr., Renee Good, Alex Pretti, Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, and Joan Sebastian Guerrero
Support funding for modern border and port-of-entry technology, staffing, and asylum-court capacity so cases are resolved in months, not years.
